claim: Craniofacial injuries comprise more than 25% of injuries reported to the National Trauma Data Bank in the US every year.
source: Craniofacial (CF) injuries comprise more than 25% of injuries reported to the National Trauma Data Bank in the US every year (Nardi et al., 2020; Wu et al., 2021; Choi et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to external literature (Nardi et al., 2020; Wu et al., 2021; Choi et al., 2020).

claim: The allograft survival rate following an iliac graft procedure is 96.1%.
source: The allograft survival rate following an iliac graft procedure is 96.1% and the risk of infection ranges from 5% to 33% (Roberts and Rosenbaum, 2012; Chaushu et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to external literature (Roberts and Rosenbaum, 2012; Chaushu et al., 2010).

claim: The risk of infection following an iliac graft procedure ranges from 5% to 33%.
source: The allograft survival rate following an iliac graft procedure is 96.1% and the risk of infection ranges from 5% to 33% (Roberts and Rosenbaum, 2012; Chaushu et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to external literature (Roberts and Rosenbaum, 2012; Chaushu et al., 2010).

claim: Revision bone graft surgeries are expensive, costing $35,000–$52,000 per patient.
source: Due to the limited supply of bone, revision bone graft surgeries are often required and are expensive ($35,000–$52,000 per patient) and cause great discomfort (Laurie et al., 1984).
evidence: Supported by citation to external literature (Laurie et al., 1984).

claim: BMP2 treatment can lead to ectopic bone growth, hypertrophy and life-threatening side effects.
source: BMP2 treatment can lead to ectopic bone growth, hypertrophy and life-threatening side effects (e.g., uncontrolled inflammation), which may accelerate bone loss (Huang et al., 2014; Tannoury and An, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to external literature (Huang et al., 2014; Tannoury and An, 2014).

claim: The use of BMP2 for the treatment of pediatric cases of CF trauma is not FDA approved due to concerns of severe swelling of the face and airways.
source: The use of BMP2 for the treatment of pediatric cases of CF trauma is not FDA approved due to concerns of severe swelling of the face and airways.
evidence: Statement about regulatory status and safety concerns.

claim: JAG1 exhibits osteo-inductive properties, as demonstrated by induction of pre-osteoblast genes like Runx2 in murine CNC cells, even when the canonical NOTCH pathway is inhibited.
source: However, we and others have demonstrated that JAG1 exhibits osteo-inductive properties, as demonstrated by induction of pre-osteoblast genes like Runx2 in murine CNC cells, even when the canonical NOTCH pathway is inhibited (Kamalakar et al., 2019; Youngstrom et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work (Kamalakar et al., 2019; Youngstrom et al., 2017).

claim: JAG1 promotes murine CNC commitment to osteoblast differentiation through a JAG1–JAK2 non-canonical signaling pathway.
source: Our recent publications further identified a JAG1–JAK2 non-canonical signaling pathway that promotes murine CNC commitment to osteoblast differentiation in mice (Kamalakar et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work (Kamalakar et al., 2019).

claim: JAG1-bds treatment significantly increased mineralization in HBO cells compared to Fc-bds-treated cells (p = 0.0107).
source: We observed significantly increased mineralization in JAG1-bds-treated samples compared to growth media-, osteogenic media-, and Fc-bds-treated (p = 0.0107) cells.
evidence: Supported by experimental data with statistical significance reported.

claim: ALPL was significantly expressed at day 7 with a 3.5-fold increase (p = 0.0004) in JAG1-bds-treated HBO1 cells compared to cells grown in growth media.
source: ALPL was significantly expressed at day 7, with a 3.5-fold increase (p = 0.0004) compared to HBO1 cells grown in growth media.
evidence: Supported by experimental data with statistical significance and fold change reported.

claim: COL1A1 expression showed a 5.1-fold increase (p = 0.0021) at 14 days in JAG1-bds-treated HBO1 cells compared to growth media conditions.
source: In contrast, significant expression levels of COL1A1 and BGLAP were observed at 14 days, with a 5.1-fold increase (p = 0.0021) of COL1A1 and a 12.3-fold increase (0.0002) of BGLAP when compared to growth media conditions.
evidence: Supported by experimental data with statistical significance and fold change reported.

claim: BGLAP expression showed a 12.3-fold increase (p = 0.0002) at 14 days in JAG1-bds-treated HBO1 cells compared to growth media conditions.
source: In contrast, significant expression levels of COL1A1 and BGLAP were observed at 14 days, with a 5.1-fold increase (p = 0.0021) of COL1A1 and a 12.3-fold increase (0.0002) of BGLAP when compared to growth media conditions.
evidence: Supported by experimental data with statistical significance and fold change reported.

claim: JAG1 can induce osteoblast commitment, differentiation, and mineralization of pediatric HBO cells.
source: These data indicate that JAG1 can induce osteoblast commitment, differentiation, and mineralization of pediatric HBO cells.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experimental data presented in Figure 1.

claim: The BV regenerated by JAG1-bds in the absence of DAPT (fold change: 1.5) was significantly higher compared to the cells alone treatment group (p = 0.0092).
source: The BV regenerated by JAG1-bds in the absence (fold change: 1.5) and presence of DAPT (fold change:1.6) was significantly higher compared to the cells alone treatment group (p = 0.0092 and 0.0021, respectively).
evidence: Supported by experimental data with statistical significance and fold change reported.

claim: The BV regenerated by JAG1-bds in the presence of DAPT (fold change: 1.6) was significantly higher compared to the cells alone treatment group (p = 0.0021).
source: The BV regenerated by JAG1-bds in the absence (fold change: 1.5) and presence of DAPT (fold change:1.6) was significantly higher compared to the cells alone treatment group (p = 0.0092 and 0.0021, respectively).
evidence: Supported by experimental data with statistical significance and fold change reported.

claim: BMP2 significantly increased regenerated BV (p = 0.0002) compared to the cells alone group.
source: As expected, BMP2 significantly increased regenerated BV (p = 0.0002) compared to the cells alone group.
evidence: Supported by experimental data with statistical significance reported.

claim: There was no sex-based difference in regenerated BV.
source: There was no sex-based difference in regenerated BV.
evidence: Observation from experimental data analysis.

claim: JAG1 can be used as a bone regenerative therapy where JAG1 induces bone regeneration independently of NOTCH canonical signaling in human cells.
source: This suggests that JAG1 can be used as a bone regenerative therapy where JAG1 induces bone regeneration independently of NOTCH canonical signaling in human cells.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experimental data showing bone regeneration with JAG1 in the presence of DAPT.

claim: A total of 448 genes were upregulated and 435 genes were downregulated in the non-canonical pathway when comparing JAG1-bds and JAG1-bds + DAPT groups to no treatment.
source: Analysis of differentially expressed genes (DEGs) in JAG1-bds and JAG1-bds + DAPT groups compared to no treatment revealed a total of 448 upregulated genes and 435 downregulated genes in the non-canonical pathway (Figure 3B, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by RNA sequencing data and analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Upregulated genes in the non-canonical pathway include genes involved in osteoblast commitment (RUNX2), matrix remodeling (MMP3), and diverse cytokines and chemokines (CCL5, CXCL1, and CXCL6).
source: These include upregulation of genes involved in osteoblast commitment (RUNX2), matrix remodeling (MMP3), and diverse cytokines and chemokines (CCL5, CXCL1, and CXCL6) as part of the non-canonical pathway (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: GO analysis of the upregulated genes in the non-canonical pathway revealed significant over-representation of GO terms associated with RUNX2, cytokine signaling, Nuclear factor kappa B (NF-κβ), and cell cycle.
source: Gene ontology (GO) analysis of the upregulated genes in the non-canonical pathway revealed significant over-representation of GO terms associated with RUNX2, cytokine signaling, Nuclear factor kappa B (NF-κβ), and cell cycle (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by GO analysis results shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The PIP3 activating AKT signaling pathway was upregulated by JAG1-bds treatment.
source: More interestingly, the PIP3 activating AKT signaling pathway was upregulated by JAG1-bds treatment, suggesting that JAG1 can activate NOTCH non-canonical signals via the AKT pathway.
evidence: Supported by RNA sequencing data and GO analysis.

claim: JAG1 induces significantly increased phosphorylation of STAT5, AKT, P38, JNK, RELA, and p70 S6K in JAG1-bds-treated cells, even in the presence of DAPT.
source: We observed significantly increased phosphorylation of multiple signaling molecules, including STAT5, AKT, P38, JNK, RELA, and p70 S6K in JAG1-bds-treated cells, even in the presence of DAPT (Figure 4).
evidence: Supported by Luminex-based multiplex assay data shown in Figure 4.

claim: S6K-18-treated samples showed partial inhibition of 50.2% of the JAG1-bds-induced mineralization (p = 0.0015).
source: S6K-18-treated samples showed partial inhibition of 50.2% of the JAG1-bds-induced mineralization (p = 0.0015) and not 100%, possibly because the NOTCH canonical pathway was not inhibited in these samples.
evidence: Supported by experimental data with statistical significance and percentage inhibition reported.

claim: Inhibition of JAG1-bds-induced mineralization by S6K-18 treatment alone was significant compared to mineralization induced by JAG1-bds alone, suggesting that the phosphorylation of p70 S6K is an essential event downstream of JAG1-NOTCH in JAG1-stimulated HBO cells.
source: Inhibition of JAG1-bds-induced mineralization by S6K-18 treatment alone was significant compared to mineralization induced by JAG1-bds alone suggesting that the phosphorylation of p70 S6K is an essential event downstream of JAG1-NOTCH in JAG1-stimulated HBO cells.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experimental data showing significant inhibition with S6K-18.

claim: While inhibition of NOTCH and p70 S6K decreased mineralization, there are no statistically significant changes in gene expression for ALPL, COL1A1, or BGLAP.
source: While inhibition of NOTCH and p70 S6K decreased mineralization in our mineralization assay, there are no statistically significant changes in gene expression for ALPL, COL1A1, or BGLAP (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: The HBO cells phenotypes are maturing into osteocytes and inhibiting p70 S6K hinders the cellular ability to mineralize but not the cell phenotype progression.
source: These results suggest that the HBO cells phenotypes are maturing into osteocytes and that inhibiting p70 S6K hinders the cellular ability to mineralize but not the cell phenotype progression.
evidence: Interpretation of experimental data showing decreased mineralization without changes in gene expression.

claim: JAG1 induces the expression of pre-osteoblast genes like Runx2 in murine CNC cells, even when the canonical NOTCH pathway is disabled using DAPT.
source: JAG1 also induces the expression of pre-osteoblast genes like Runx2 in murine CNC cells, even when the canonical NOTCH pathway is disabled using DAPT (Kamalakar et al., 2019; Youngstrom et al., 2017), and further promotes CNC cell commitment to osteoblast differentiation via a JAG1–JAK2 non-canonical signaling pathway (Kamalakar et al., 2019; Youngstrom et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work (Kamalakar et al., 2019; Youngstrom et al., 2017).

claim: JAG1 has been shown to induce survival and proliferation of human mesenchymal stem cells.
source: JAG1 has previously been shown to induce survival and proliferation of human mesenchymal stem cells, which are osteoblast precursors and various other human cell types, for example LNCaP which is a prostate cancer cell line, glioma cells, and intestinal epithelial cells during progression of colorectal cancer (Pannequin et al., 2009; Purow et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to external literature (Pannequin et al., 2009; Purow et al., 2005).

claim: Tissue culture plate surface-immobilized JAG1 stimulated osteoblast proliferation and differentiation in iliac bone-derived cells.
source: Osathanon et al. showed that tissue culture plate surface-immobilized JAG1-stimulated osteoblast proliferation and differentiation in iliac bone-derived cells (Osathanon et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to external literature (Osathanon et al., 2019).

claim: The ability of Fc-bds to stimulate mineralization in vitro is previously described in the literature but has not been found to be osteogenic in vivo.
source: The ability of Fc-bds to stimulate mineralization in vitro is previously described in the literature but has not been found to be osteogenic in vivo (Kamalakar et al., 2019; Kamalakar et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work (Kamalakar et al., 2019; Kamalakar et al., 2021).

claim: Intermittent treatment with bone-regenerative therapeutics, like PTH, has been shown to lead to anabolic increase in bone mineral density.
source: Intermittent treatment with bone-regenerative therapeutics, like PTH (Kamalakar et al., 2019; Nardi et al., 2020; Wu et al., 2021; Choi et al., 2020; Kumar et al., 2016; Grover et al., 2011; Roberts and Rosenbaum, 2012; Kakabadze et al., 2017; Chim et al., 2010; Chaushu et al., 2010; Dahlin and Johansson, 2011; Baumhauer et al., 2014; Laurie et al., 1984; De Sousa, 2010; Shah et al., 2021; Rowshan et al., 2010; Elsalanty and Genecov, 2009; Nosho et al., 2020; Takayama et al., 2017; Albanese et al., 2013; Seto et al., 2006; Zuk, 2008; Huang et al., 2014; Tannoury and An, 2014; Zanotti and Canalis, 2012; Nobta et al., 2005; Regan and Long, 2013; Youngstrom et al., 2017; Phelps et al., 2012; Bouxsein et al., 2010; Love et al., 2014; Zhao et al., 2014; Sayers et al., 2021; Thomas et al., 2022; Fowler et al., 2012; Langdahl et al., 2018) has been shown to lead to anabolic increase in bone mineral density.
evidence: Supported by extensive citations to external literature.

claim: The inhibition of NOTCH canonical signaling in mesenchymal stem cells using DAPT has been shown previously to enhance osteogenesis.
source: The inhibition of NOTCH canonical signaling in mesenchymal stem cells using DAPT has been shown previously to enhance osteogenesis (Luo et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to external literature (Luo et al., 2019).

claim: A rheumatoid Arthritis C57BL/6 SCID mouse model carrying a human TNF transgene when treated with intermittent doses of DAPT showed improved bone regeneration.
source: A rheumatoid Arthritis C57BL/6 SCID mouse model carrying a human TNF transgene when treated with intermittent doses of DAPT showed improved bone regeneration (Zhang et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to external literature (Zhang et al., 2014).

claim: RUNX2 is commonly known to be expressed by osteoblasts as a sign of their recruitment into the lineage.
source: RUNX2 is commonly known to be expressed by osteoblasts as a sign of their recruitment into the lineage (Komori, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to external literature (Komori, 2010).

claim: MMP3 is abundantly expressed by osteoblasts and is an important regulator of bone remodeling.
source: MMP3 is also abundantly expressed by osteoblasts and is an important regulator of bone remodeling. MMP3 is an enzyme that is essential in the processing of collagen on bone surface, which in turn is necessary for osteoclast recruitment and bone resorption (Jehan et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to external literature (Jehan et al., 2022).

claim: Chemokine CCL5 is abundantly expressed by osteoblasts, and it is involved in recruitment of osteoblast progenitor cells.
source: Chemokine CCL5 is abundantly expressed by osteoblasts, and it is also involved in recruitment of osteoblast progenitor cells (Brylka and Schinke, 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to external literature (Brylka and Schinke, 2019).

claim: CXCL1 serves as an intermediate during PTH/PTH1R-induced differentiation of osteoblasts.
source: PTH/parathyroid hormone 1 receptor (PTH1R) induces the differentiation of osteoblasts, and it has been shown that CXCL1 serves as an intermediate during this process (Onan et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to external literature (Onan et al., 2009).

claim: RELA is known to be a radiation-induced pro-survival factor in human osteoblastic cells.
source: RELA was also upregulated, and it is known to be a radiation-induced pro-survival factor in human osteoblastic cells (Xiao et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to external literature (Xiao et al., 2009).

claim: STAT5 is essential for AKT–p70 S6K activity during lymphocyte proliferation in patients with leukemias and lymphomas.
source: For example, the WNT pathway cross-talks with the NOTCH canonical pathway during vascular morphogenesis (Caliceti et al., 2014). Furthermore, previous reports have shown that STAT5 is essential for AKT–p70 S6K activity during lymphocyte proliferation in patients with leukemias and lymphomas (Lockyer et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to external literature (Lockyer et al., 2007).

claim: The P38 pathway has been shown to activate the mTOR–p70 S6K pathway during oxidative stress in mouse embryonic fibroblast cells.
source: Similarly, the P38 pathway has been shown to activate the mammalian target of rapamycin (mTOR)–p70 S6K pathway during oxidative stress in mouse embryonic fibroblast cells which culminates in upregulation of antioxidative enzymes that assist in reactive oxygen species removal and thereafter increase cell survival (Gutiérrez-Uzquiza et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to external literature (Gutiérrez-Uzquiza et al., 2012).

claim: JNK phosphorylates p70 S6K to induce osteoblast proliferation and differentiation of MC3T3 cells.
source: Also shown previously, JNK phosphorylates p70 S6K to induce osteoblast proliferation and differentiation of MC3T3 cells, and can crosstalk in other physiological systems, for example, during hepatocyte proliferation (Bouxsein et al., 2010; Love et al., 2014; Zhao et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to external literature (Bouxsein et al., 2010; Love et al., 2014; Zhao et al., 2014).

claim: AKT–mTOR–p70 S6K, ERK, and NF-κB were involved together in proliferation of osteosarcoma cells and these pathways could be inhibited by caffeine thereby decreasing tumor burden.
source: A study by Miwa et al., in 2012, showed that AKT–mTOR–p70 S6K, extracellular signal-regulated kinases (ERK), and NF-κB were involved together in proliferation of osteosarcoma cells and these pathways could be inhibited by caffeine thereby decreasing tumor burden (Miwa et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to external literature (Miwa et al., 2012).

claim: p70 S6K is an enzyme that phosphorylates the S6 ribosomal protein to initiate protein synthesis which supports growth, proliferation, differentiation, and glucose homeostasis of cells.
source: p70 S6K is an enzyme that phosphorylates the S6 ribosomal protein to initiate protein synthesis which supports growth, proliferation, differentiation, and glucose homeostasis of cells (Ruvinsky et al., 2005; Ruvinsky and Meyuhas, 2006; Ruvinsky et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to external literature (Ruvinsky et al., 2005; Ruvinsky and Meyuhas, 2006; Ruvinsky et al., 2009).

claim: JAG1 has a profound NOTCH non-canonical effect on HBO cells that stimulates HBO cell-osteoblast commitment and differentiation leading to HBO-cell-induced bone formation.
source: Collectively, these data suggest that JAG1 has a profound NOTCH non-canonical effect on HBO cells that stimulates HBO cell-osteoblast commitment and differentiation leading to HBO-cell-induced bone formation.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from RNA sequencing and pathway analysis data.

claim: JAG1 promotes human pediatric osteoblast commitment and bone formation through p70 S6K phosphorylation.
source: Delivering pediatric human bone-derived osteoblast-like cells to an in vivo murine bone loss model of a critically sized cranial defect, we identified that JAGGED1 promotes human pediatric osteoblast commitment and bone formation through p70 S6K phosphorylation.
evidence: Conclusion stated in the abstract based on experimental findings.

claim: Craniofacial bone development primarily occurs through intramembranous ossification.
source: CF bone development primarily occurs through intramembranous ossification, a process where pre-osteoblasts mineralize directly, without a cartilage intermediate, making it distinct from long bone development (endochondral ossification) (Shah et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to external literature (Shah et al., 2021).

claim: Intramembranous ossification recruits cranial neural crest (CNC) cells as osteoblast precursors during CF bone development.
source: Intramembranous ossification recruits cranial neural crest (CNC) cells as osteoblast precursors during CF bone development (Shah et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to external literature (Shah et al., 2021).

claim: HBO cells were derived from healthy fibulas of seven pediatric subjects.
source: HBO cell lines were derived from healthy fibulas of seven pediatric subjects under appropriate Institutional Review Board approval.
evidence: Description of experimental methods.

claim: Six- to eight-week-old male and female NOD.Cg-Prkdcscid/J mice were used for in vivo experiments.
source: We performed all in vivo experiments using procedural guidelines with appropriate approvals from the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee of Emory University (#PROTO201700263). Six- to eight-week-old male and female NOD.Cg-Prkdcscid/J mice (The Jackson Laboratory, 001303) were used.
evidence: Description of experimental methods.

claim: A second dose of the hydrogels encapsulating HBO cells and Dynabead-bound JAG1 were administered as transcutaneous injections during week 4.
source: A second dose of the hydrogels encapsulating HBO cells and Dynabead-bound JAG1 were administered as transcutaneous injections during week 4 to continue the bone regenerative action of JAG1.
evidence: Description of experimental methods.

claim: Skulls were harvested at week 8, fixed using 10% neutral buffered formalin and imaged with µCT.
source: Skulls were then harvested at week 8, fixed using 10% neutral buffered formalin (VWR, 89370-094) and imaged with µCT.
evidence: Description of experimental methods.

claim: HBO primary cell lines 2, 6, and 7 from separate individuals were selected for in vivo experiments based on similar growth and passage characteristics.
source: HBO primary cell lines 2, 6, and 7 from separate individuals were selected for these experiments based on similar growth and passage characteristics.
evidence: Description of experimental methods and selection criteria.

claim: There was no difference in bone regeneration between an Empty Defect model (no HBO cells) and a Cells Alone group in an initial pilot study.
source: An initial pilot study also demonstrated no difference in bone regeneration between an Empty Defect model (no HBO cells) and a Cells Alone group (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by pilot study data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Mice treated with cells alone had less collagen production compared to mice treated with BMP2, JAG1-bds, and JAG1-bds + DAPT.
source: These results corroborate what was revealed with the Masson trichrome staining, that mice treated with cells alone had less collagen production (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemical staining data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: Expression of RUNX2 and SP7 was not significantly altered across all conditions and time points in HBO1 cells.
source: Expression of RUNX2 and SP7 was not significantly altered across all conditions and time points (not shown).
evidence: Observation from experimental data (not shown in figures).

claim: Some mineralization is observed in the osteogenic media and Fc-bds conditions, but there were no significant increases in osteogenic gene expression.
source: Interestingly, while some mineralization is observed in the osteogenic media and Fc-bds (Figure 1A) conditions, there were no significant increases in osteogenic gene expression (Figure 1C).
evidence: Observation from experimental data shown in Figures 1A and 1C.
